You are deriving structured "systems" from the distilled summary of a guitar method book.

A SYSTEM is a graph-with-rules. It has:
  - members[]: the taxonomy (the things this system operates over — chord
    types, position regions, voicing categories, scale forms, etc.)
  - traversal_rules[]: how you MOVE between members (preference for
    common-tone voice motion, pivot-finger shifts, position continuity,
    etc.)
  - modification_rules[]: how you ALTER a member (substitution lattices,
    voicing density changes, omission policies, color-tone requirements,
    etc.)

Each rule carries an `engine_payload` with a `kind` field. The kind is
either ONE of these 12 names (use exactly as spelled):

  PositionContinuity, VoiceMotion, StringSetTransition, SymmetryMovement,
  FamilyCoherence, SubstitutionExpand, DensityFloor, DensityCeiling,
  OmissionAllow, ColorToneRequire, NCTHarmonization, TextureCycle

OR a `_pending:<short-kebab-slug>` placeholder when no name in the list
clearly fits. When in doubt, USE `_pending:`. Do not stretch a name to fit.
The formal definitions of these kinds are pending (#298); your job today
is to pick the best label or honestly admit uncertainty.

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  {
    "master_id": "<from config>",
    "work_id": "<from config>",
    "systems": [
      {
        "id": "<master_id>:<work_id>:<system-slug>",
        "name": "<full system name>",
        "summary": "<one-paragraph prose>",
        "members": [
          { "id": "<slug>", "name": "<full name>", "summary": "<optional>" }
        ],
        "traversal_rules": [
          {
            "id": "<slug>",
            "name": "<full name>",
            "summary": "<one sentence>",
            "engine_payload": { "kind": "<kind-name or _pending:slug>" }
          }
        ],
        "modification_rules": [...]
      }
    ]
  }

Guidance:
- Three-segment system ids. Slug is kebab-case. Example:
  "benson:method-vol-1-chord-construction:harmonized-scale"
- Aim for 1-4 systems per book. A book usually has ONE central system plus
  optionally a few smaller ones.
- A system MUST have non-empty members AND at least one rule (traversal
  or modification) — empty systems are not useful.
- members[], traversal_rules[], modification_rules[] are all optional fields
  per the schema, but a real system has at least members + one rule kind.
- If the book teaches a system you can't structure as members+rules,
  describe it in `summary` and leave members/rules empty rather than
  inventing.

EVERY rule (traversal_rule, modification_rule, preference) MUST carry a
`references[]` array with at least one entry pointing back at the chapter
quote that backs the rule. Reference shape:

  { "chapter_n": <int>, "topic": "<topic label from chapter file>",
    "quote_excerpt": "<5-15 word snippet of the source quote>",
    "page": <int, optional> }

If a rule has no source quote it does not belong in the systems-draft —
write it into the system's `summary` field or omit it. References make
every kind assignment auditable; without them, this draft cannot be
reviewed against the source.

# Howard Roberts' *Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks*: A Distillation

Howard Roberts' *Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks* is a rigidly disciplined, systems-driven method for building jazz improvisation technique on guitar. Its central axiom, announced in Chapter 1 and restated throughout, is that **speed is a byproduct of accuracy** — never a goal in itself. Every structural choice in the book flows from this premise: the equipment standards, the practice schedule, the metronome doctrine, and the tempo objectives are all downstream of a prior commitment to precision. The book's arc moves from physical setup (Chapters 1–2), through harmonic and melodic vocabulary (Chapters 3–4), into line construction (Chapters 5–6), and finally into the disciplinary and psychological framework required to execute the 20-week program (Chapters 7–9).

Roberts begins with equipment as pedagogy. Chapter 1 prescribes **medium-heavy string gauge** (.012 minimum), **medium-high action**, and **medium to heavy celluloid picks** — not for tone, but to build resistance that develops left-hand strength and right-hand control. Three non-guitar tools are equally mandatory: a **metronome**, a **tape recorder**, and a **timer**. These devices externalize the method's three core feedback loops — time, self-monitoring, and session discipline. The **note clarity standard** (every note must ring loud and clear across the entire fingerboard) functions as the primary diagnostic for whether setup and technique are correct.

Chapter 2 identifies the right hand as the primary limiting factor for improvisers and establishes **flexibility** as the governing mechanical principle. Roberts explicitly rejects rigid anchoring systems — elbow, wrist, or pick-guard anchors — as speed ceilings under tension. Left-hand mechanics require perpendicular fretting (like piano hammers), thumb centered on the neck, and economical finger lift to balance noise control with efficiency. The non-negotiable technical law of the chapter is **left-right hand synchronization**: even a fractional flam between hands is a failure state, diagnosed by playing slowly across the full fingerboard, and corrected by a flat left-wrist posture that reduces strain and enables consistency.

Chapters 3 and 4 build the harmonic and melodic vocabulary. Chapter 3 teaches **key centers** — the understanding that chord progressions belong to a key generated by stacking a major or minor scale in thirds — and the **five movable fingerboard patterns** organized by **finger-per-fret** mechanics, with tonics visually circled. Connection between patterns is achieved through three moves: **position skips, stretching, and sliding on half steps**. Chapter 4 then supplies the melodic toolkit: six scale types (diatonic major, harmonic minor, melodic minor, diminished, whole-tone, major pentatonic), **arpeggios** as chord-outlining lines that move at steeper angles than scales, and **interval skips** as the primary antidote to scalar monotony. Roberts prescribes limiting consecutive scale tones to **3–4 notes in one direction** before changing direction or introducing a skip, and demands that interval skips be derived *diatonically* — respecting the key's half-steps — to preserve tonality. **Common tones** function as a relief technique from constant motion.

Chapter 5 introduces the **20-week program structure**: six days of practice per week, 50-minute daily sessions, targeting ♩ = 126. The program divides into three phases — **duple time** (Weeks 1–6, eighth notes), **triple time** (Weeks 8–13, triplet feels), and **tempo solidification with legato techniques** (Weeks 15–17). **Legato techniques** — hammer-ons, pull-offs, and glissandi — are introduced strategically in the final phase because they allow multiple pitches per pick stroke, accelerating apparent speed without increasing picking effort. The appendix's numbered reference lines (1-A, 1-B, etc.) ground each week's abstract structure in notated musical content, functioning as models rather than prescriptions.

Chapter 6 addresses the psychological and structural practices required to execute the program. Core techniques include **melody sketch over changes** (pre-planning structural scaffolding), **question and answer form** (the foundational improvisational pattern), and **sing before playing** (embedding melodic ideas through the ear before the hand). Roberts introduces his **growth plateau cycle**: the counterintuitive principle that *subjective struggle signals active neurological development*, while *felt fluency signals a rest period*. Students are explicitly warned not to quit when progress feels stalled — that feeling is the learning. **Memorizing chord changes** is non-negotiable, freeing cognitive bandwidth for real-time musical decision-making. Informal **noodling** is validated as a legitimate, low-pressure practice mode. The chapter closes with an iron contract: the program demands **exact execution without deviation**, and schedule consistency is the ultimate load-bearing requirement.

Chapters 7–9 hammer the disciplinary and diagnostic framework. The **eighth-notes-only rule** and **alternate picking requirement** (Chapters 7–8) isolate picking mechanics by removing rhythmic and technical variables. Roberts' **21-day permanent imprinting threshold** asserts that maintaining a tempo for 21 consecutive days locks it into the nervous system as a permanent motor reflex. The **metronome-as-tracker** doctrine reframes the device as a progress recorder rather than a speed target. Chapter 7 also names several diagnostic failure modes: **awkward tempos between feel zones** (certain tempo ranges are structurally uncomfortable and should be pushed through, not practiced), **environmental tuning interference** (auditing room conditions before attributing failure to technique), and **blame attribution** (the discipline of identifying the correct hand before attempting any fix). Chapter 9 closes the book's conceptual arc by insisting that all technical training exists to serve **spontaneous invention** — the model solos are reference material, not blueprints. The final ethos is "every man for himself": technique is the enabler, and the goal is always the immediate, unmediated realization of the student's own musical imagination.

## Key center definition

> When a given major or minor scale is stacked upon itself in thirds as shown in Example 1,
> it creates harmony characteristic of that scale.

> Eb 7 is a V chord (Dominant 7 type) which only appears once in any given major key,
> always as the V chord, and therefore, only one possibility, the V of Ab.

**Significance (p. 7).** This teaches the key analytical shortcut that the dominant seventh chord uniquely identifies a single key, making it the most decisive chord for key-center determination.

## Using key center brackets

> In all studies to follow, the key centers have been bracketed above the
> chord progression. Observe these key centers with care and for each new one, move your
> hand to a convenient fingering pattern for that particular scale and do your improvising
> in that region of the guitar.

**Significance (p. 8).** This gives the student a direct, actionable physical instruction for how to use key-center analysis while improvising over the book's exercises.

## Five movable scale patterns

> There are five such patterns for any given scale. And each
> of these five are movable up or down the neck to the selected key or, they may be connected
> to increase the range.

**Significance (p. 8).** This establishes the five-pattern framework that organizes the entire fingerboard system taught in the chapter.

## Playing changes by ear

> In addition to being able to logically calculate key centers fron an analysis of the progres-
> sion, the ability to play over changes by ear, can be viewed as the ideal end result.

**Significance (p. 8).** This sets the ear as the ultimate goal beyond intellectual analysis, orienting the student's long-term practice direction.

## Finger-per-fret mechanics

> There are five tone patterns for the diatonic major scale. The mechanics of the fingerings
> center around the use of a finger per fret, although in most cases it becomes necessary to
> reach out of position one fret either above or below the basic position with the first or
> fourth finger.

**Significance (p. 9).** This defines the physical left-hand rule governing all five patterns, giving students the core technique underlying every fingering diagram in the chapter.

## Patterns cover full fingerboard

> When these patterns are laid end to end, they cover the entire finger-
> board for any one key.

**Significance (p. 9).** This tells the student that mastering all five patterns yields complete neck coverage, establishing why all five must be learned.

## Modifying patterns for minor

> the relative harmonic minor scales can be quickly
> learned by simply sharping the fifth scale step of the diatonic scales, which is the same as
> __sharping the seventh of the relative minor scales.

**Significance (p. 9).** This provides the single-note modification rule that derives harmonic minor from the already-learned diatonic patterns, dramatically reducing new memorization.

## Arpeggios within scale pattern

> arpeggios will be easier to handle if they are played within a scale pattern that cor
> responds to the key center from which the chord is derived, e.g. the progression Dm7,

## common tones defined

> A common tone is a note that is common to two or more chords, a very simple technique
> but not to be overlooked, i.e. when playing non-stop eighth notes, or triplets, etc., it
> is not necessary to keep the line moving at all times. The line can be flattened out ---
> a nice relief from excessive vertical movement.

**Significance (p. 11).** Defines the common-tone technique and explicitly instructs the student to use sustained notes as a relief device rather than constant melodic motion.

## scales create smooth lines

> Create smooth rolling lines.

**Significance (p. 11).** States the core functional purpose of scale usage in line construction before presenting each scale type.

## diatonic major scale half steps

> The Diatonic Major Scale (with } steps between the 3rd/4th and 7th/8th scale steps

**Significance (p. 11).** Identifies the defining structural characteristic of the major scale — its two half-step positions — which underpins all diatonic harmony.

## harmonic minor scale structure

> The Relative Harmonic Minor Scale (with } steps between the 2nd/3rd and 7th/8th scale
> steps.)

**Significance (p. 12).** Distinguishes harmonic minor from natural minor by specifying its unique half-step intervals, essential for correct scale construction.

## melodic minor ascending/descending rule

> The Relative Melodic Minor Scale (with } steps between the 2nd/3rd and 7th/8th scale steps
> ascending and reverting back to the natural minor descending. NOTE: The ascending and
> descending rules here are a technicality, which in the final analysis may be disregarded
> in favor of the existant bar harmony

**Significance (p. 12).** Presents the traditional ascending/descending rule but immediately qualifies it with a practical override based on bar harmony, teaching harmonic context over rote rule-following.

## diminished scale usage

> The Diminished Scale (symetrical, consecutive whole step and half steps) most commonly
> used over dominant 'th chords or diminished chords.

**Significance (p. 12).** Defines the diminished scale's symmetrical construction and specifies the chord contexts where it is applied, giving the student both structure and usage guidance.

## whole tone scale usage

> The Whole Tone Scale (symetrical, consecutive whole steps) most commonly used over
> dominant 7th chords.

**Significance (p. 12).** Defines the whole-tone scale's symmetrical structure and pins its idiomatic use to dominant 7th chords.

## major pentatonic scale definition

> The Major Pentatonic Scale (same as diatonic major with the active tones 3rd and 7th
> left out). When harmonized creates inversions of a Major 6/9 chord, with little gravi-
> tational pull toward any key center "depending on the usage".

**Significance (p. 13).** Defines the pentatonic scale by subtraction from the major scale and explains its ambiguous tonal gravity, which is the key reason it is useful across multiple harmonic contexts.

## arpeggios defined and contrasted

> Arpeggios are specifically chords, broken up into single notes. They are effective in out-
> lining the bar harmony and offer a nice contrast to scale movement as they create smooth
> rolling lines, at sharper angles than scales.

**Significance (p. 13).** Defines arpeggios functionally and positions them relative to scales — same smooth quality but at steeper melodic angles — establishing the contrast the student should hear and exploit.

## interval skips dramatic effect

> Interval skips create sharp, dramatic lines. An interval is the distance between any two
> notes, Large interval skips can be a valuable tool for creating interesting lines and can
> have a dramatic effect in breaking up the monotomy of excessive scale movement.

**Significance (p. 13).** Identifies interval skips as the primary antidote to scale monotony and names the dramatic quality they produce, motivating the student to practice them.

## scale intervals avoid parallel

> Any
> sequence of interval skips, 3rds, 7ths, S9ths, etc., can easily be applied to a key center
> by playing scale intervals that take into account the half steps of the scale, thus, resulting
> in combinations of major and minor 3rds or major and minor 7ths (not, parallel 3rds, 7ths,
> etc.)

**Significance (p. 13).** Instructs the student to derive interval skips diatonically rather than in parallel, which is the critical technique for keeping skips in key.

## breaking up scale-like playing

> A most common complaint of beginning improvisors is that their playing tends to become
> too scale-like. One solution to this could be to stop playing things that "sound" like
> scales, for example, as an exercise; don't play more than 3 or 4 scale tones in the same
> direction, e.g. this type of scale movement creates interval skips, small and large, thus
> breaking up the scale effect.

**Significance (p. 13).** Names the most common beginner improvisation flaw and gives a concrete, actionable rule — no more than 3 or 4 consecutive scale tones in one direction — to overcome it.

**Significance (p. 16).** Validates informal, low-pressure practice as a legitimate learning mode, giving students permission to count passive playing time.

## melody sketch over changes

> Sometimes it's helpful to sketch out a very simple melody line over the changes, i.e. half note, quarter notes, halves, etc. Let this line run through your head as a basic melody and play "fills" around it. This wil! at least get your line started with some form.

**Significance (p. 16).** Provides a concrete structural entry point for building a solo line when the student is stuck.

## question and answer form

> A very common form for building a solo line is: QUESTION AND ANSWER. When this Q/A routine re-occurs, it is generally called a sequence.

**Significance (p. 16).** Names and defines the Q/A sequence concept, which is a foundational structural principle for melodic improvisation.

## sing before playing

> Listen to the "pre-recorded changes" and sing the solo the wa'

**Significance (p. 16).** Directs students to internalize melodic ideas vocally before executing them on the instrument, a core ear-to-hand principle.

**Significance (p. 16).** Teaches students to recognize and break habitual patterns in real time without interrupting the flow of improvisation.

## fixing technique flams

> HANGUPS: Play very slowly and listen carefully for any flams. Use all up strokes. Make each note sound as loud and strong as any other. Now use all up strokes, scales, interval skips. Now use consecutive down and up strokes. Now reverse to all up (on the down beat) and down (on the up beat) strokes.

**Significance (p. 16).** Prescribes a specific diagnostic and corrective picking sequence for eliminating timing flams and uneven note dynamics.

## warm-up and string travel

> At the beginning of each practice session, warm up for 5 minutes by playing notes all over the fingerboard. Play very slowly, low, high, and medium pitches, to develop a feel for string travel at a given picking area. Notes played high up on the neck have a much greater string travel than the low ones and can create coordination problems between the left and right hands. Both must attack the string simultaneously.

**Significance (p. 16).** Explains why register-spanning warm-up matters mechanically — string travel distance varies by position and directly causes left/right-hand synchronization failures.

## blaming the wrong hand

> A most common mistake is to blame the left hand when the right hand is at fault, or vice versa. Watch out for this.

**Significance (p. 17).** Warns against a universal misdiagnosis habit that causes students to practice the wrong hand and never fix the actual problem.

## memorizing chord changes

> Get the progression off the paper and into your head as soon as possible. Memorizing the chord changes allows you to focus all of your attention on what you are playing rather than reading the music.

**Significance (p. 17).** States the direct cognitive reason for memorization: reading splits attention away from real-time musical decision-making.

## program adherence requirements

> The objectives put forth in this book are attainable only if the reader follows each step of the program without deviation from the schedule (that means no missed days, hours shortened, time frames disobeyed, key centers missed, introducing hammer-on's, pull-off's, before stated, playin tted eighth six- teenth notes instead of eighth notes, etc., etc.) If you do it, you get It. you don't, you don't.

**Significance (p. 17).** Establishes the method's non-negotiable contract with the student, specifying exact categories of deviation that will undermine results.

## growth plateau cycle

> In the Growth Process, we all go through periods in which we are activating new nerve junctures, both in the brain and throughout other parts of the body. This type of growth work draws a tremendous amount of systemic energies. The overall physical feeling is like pulling a train uphill, and the psychological spin-off is the feeling that we are getting nowhere. This will persist for some period of time. We then tend to go into a natural state of rest, "a plateau." During this rest period, we tend to feel that we have the world by the tail and great progress is taking place. Actually the reverse is true. The progress was made during the uphill climb, not during the rest period.

**Significance (p. 17).** Inverts students' intuitive reading of their own progress by explaining that subjective difficulty signals real growth while felt fluency signals a plateau, preventing them from mistaking struggle for failure.

## constant practice regimen

> So, on and on it goes, but your practice regimen must remain constant.

**Significance (p. 17).** Delivers the actionable takeaway from the plateau discussion: the only correct response to the cycle is an unwavering schedule.

## metronome as progress tracker

> Do not set your metronome to a desired speed and try to rise to meet it. Rather,
> use the metronome only to track your progress. Keep a daily record of your
> tempos in the boxes provided. (NOTE: Your tempo may vary slower or faster
> from day to day. This is to be expected.)

**Significance (p. 19).** Reframes the metronome's pedagogical role from a target to a diagnostic tool, a conceptual distinction that directly shapes how students approach daily practice.

## practice regularity imperative

> Do each project lesson for six consecutive days, with one day off. Avoid
> skipping a day, for whatever reason. The effect is hazardous to progress.
> Regularity is essential. Follow the steps faithfully as given.

**Significance (p. 19).** States the method's non-negotiable structure for skill consolidation and explicitly warns that irregular practice is harmful, not merely suboptimal.

## key center analysis flexibility

> The key centers bracketed in the chord progressions represent only one analysis
> of the progression. Other views may be applied as well. For example, you will
> encounter key center brackets in which a given chord could be viewed as a III
> or V1 chord of one key, but indicated as a I! chord of another. In these situations,
> one's individual preference can prevail. It's just a matter of where you want the
> change of tonality to occur. Also, there are almost unlimited scale and chord
> substitution possibilities. Feel free to use any harmonic devices at your disposal.
> If they're right, they will sound right and if they're wrong, you will know it
> immediately.

**Significance (p. 19).** Teaches the student that harmonic analysis is interpretive rather than prescriptive and introduces the ear as the final arbiter of substitution choices.

## tempo goals vs. accuracy

> Care should be taken not to sacrifice accuracy
> and precision in order to meet the tempo goals.. These will always come In time.
> "The tempo objective plan is Symmetrical, but the learning curve is not.

**Significance (p. 19).** Articulates a core pedagogical principle that accuracy precedes speed and that the learning curve is inherently asymmetric, countering the student's natural impulse to rush toward tempo targets.

## alternate picking stroke equality

> Use Alternate Picking only. No two strokes in the same direction, i.e. strive
> to make up strokes sound as strong as down strokes.

**Significance (p. 19).** Defines the technical goal of alternate picking not merely as direction alternation but as dynamic equality between up and down strokes, which is the actual mechanical challenge students must internalize.

## spontaneous invention over examples

> Remember! This example and all other examples for the project
> lessons are models of the type of sold line to be improvised. The
> important consideration is the spontaneous invention of your own
> solo line. The point of the project lessons is to hone your tech-
> nique to a level that will facilitate and not hinder the immediate
> reproduction of any and all of your musical ideas. Use the exam-
> ples as source material and for reference, but when doing the
> project lessons, it's "every man for himself".

**Significance (p. 27).** Articulates the core didactic principle that technique training serves spontaneous musical expression, defining the purpose of practice as enabling — not constraining — improvisation.
